body:
Tested on 4.4 beta2, can confirm that I also observe this behavior.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/d000f11b-eb50-441b-9fe2-705973fadd44)

These wrong results seem to happen only if the ShapeCast is already inside of what it collides with. If you are outside any colliders and cast the shape into any of the boxes (target position not `Vector3.ZERO`), results are correct. 
Maybe this behavior is somewhat expected?

I believe it's returning a contact point on the other shape, which is a point where they'd be touching if the shapecast shape were moved out of it by the shortest displacement possible(?) so that they aren't intersecting anymore.  When two shapes are deeply embedded in each other sometimes shoving out the 'side' becomes the shortest displacement.

> If you are outside any colliders and cast the shape into any of the boxes (target position not `Vector3.ZERO`), results are correct.

If the target position is != (0,0,0) and the shapecast starts outside of colliders, we only get the first collision point, as far as I understand. You can't get multiple collision points this way. So it's not suitable for the required use case. Especially since even in the described failure case, the shapecast correctly finds the first and last point no matter what, the problem is only with the middle points.



> I believe it's returning a contact point on the other shape, which is a point where they'd be touching if the shapecast shape were moved out of it by the shortest displacement possible(?) so that they aren't intersecting anymore. When two shapes are deeply embedded in each other sometimes shoving out the 'side' becomes the shortest displacement.

So you're saying that this is a consequence of the engine's mathematical approach to intersection resolution? ShapeCast3D returns points where the shapes would touch after splitting, not the actual entry points, which leads to unintuitive results for complex intersections, right?

Does this mean it will be very difficult to fix?

Why do both GodotPhysics and Jolt have this problem? Do both physics engines handle shapecasts the same way or does Godot have a layer on top of the physics engines where this bug occurs?

Yeah I agree with stoofin: the collision points shown are where the ShapeCast would meet the StaticBody if the ShapeCast only had superficial contact with the StaticBody.

> ShapeCast3D returns points where the shapes would touch after splitting, not the actual entry points [...]

I think non-deformable Physics objects (that should collide with each other) shouldn't have "entry" points - upon the first contact, there should be a collision response precisely to avoid one body entering another. I'm not sure what you mean by "splitting".

From the looks of it you'll need to come up with a custom solution, your use case seems to not be what ShapeCast is built to deliver.

I checked _PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D.collide_shape_ and it gives the same point positions as ShapeCast. After stoofin's explanation, everything falls into place. Probably, this is not a bug, but the result of a misunderstanding of the purposes for which ShapeCast exists.

The documentation is misleading. It clearly states that the method will return collision points "_where the shape intersects the colliding object_". From what was written, I expected that the points would be **directly within the shape**: something like a raycast, but volumetric and with the ability to collect many collisions one after another. In fact, it looks for contact points where they would be if the shape were moved from the obstacle outside of it in the shortest direction. Nowhere does it say anything about this. I was absolutely sure that this was a bug and should not work like that. Only stoofin's explanation put everything into place.

ShapeCast is good for checking before spawning a character if it will be inside a collider and if so, you can move it outside the collider. But not as a volumetric RayCast. I found that _PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D.cast_motion_ is better for this purpose. After it finds a collision point, you can _cast_motion_ again from that point in the same direction and repeat in a loop until the distance is exhausted. And thus collect all the intersection points on the casting path.

_cast_motion_ does not detect collisions inside colliders (like raycast with _hit_from_inside_ disabled), so it can be cast again from the collision point in the same direction. _cast_motion_ is more like a volumetric RayCast than ShapeCast does.

I think if no one has any objections, the request will be closed. But it would be nice if someone could add to the documentation of _ShapeCast_ and _PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D.collide_shape_ to better explain how this function works and what results to expect. It's probably worth opening a issue request at https://github.com/godotengine/godot-docs/issues, but I don't have time right now, so someone else can do it to avoid further confusion.
